questions.text: A utility function represents preferences when it assigns

options.a: numbers equal to the market cost of each bundle.
options.b: higher numbers to more-preferred bundles and lower numbers to less-preferred bundles.
options.c: cardinal units that are comparable across all consumers.
options.d: the same number to all affordable bundles.

questions.text: The utility concept used in standard consumer theory in these slides is primarily

options.b: cardinal: utility differences have a unique behavioral meaning.
options.c: interpersonal: one consumer’s utility can be compared directly with another’s.
options.d: ordinal: only the ranking of bundles matters.

questions.text: If A ≻ B, a utility representation u must satisfy

options.b: u(A) < u(B).
options.c: u(A) = u(B).
options.d: u(A) − u(B) = 1 exactly.

questions.text: Why is a utility representation generally not unique?

options.a: Market prices determine only one possible utility scale.
options.b: Utility must be measured in euros, which can be converted to other currencies.
options.c: Any strictly increasing transformation preserves the ranking of bundles.
options.d: Preferences are assumed to be incomplete.

questions.text: A monotonic transformation f(u) is one that

options.b: maps every utility level to the same number.
options.c: must be linear with slope exactly one.
options.d: preserves order: if u1 > u2, then f(u1) > f(u2).

questions.text: A differentiable transformation f(u) is strictly increasing where

options.b: df/du < 0.
options.c: df/du > 0.
options.d: f(u) = 0 for all u.

questions.text: If v(x1,x2) = f(u(x1,x2)) and f is strictly increasing, then v and u

options.b: can represent the same preferences only if f is the identity function.
options.c: represent the same preferences.
options.d: must have identical numerical marginal utilities.

questions.text: Cardinal utility would attach behavioral significance to

options.b: the size of utility differences between bundles.
options.c: only the ranking of bundles.
options.d: the slope of the budget line but not preferences.

questions.text: In standard consumer-choice theory, cardinal utility is unnecessary because

options.b: prices already measure utility directly.
options.c: choice behavior can be described using only ordinal rankings.
options.d: all consumers have the same utility function.

questions.text: A utility function can be viewed geometrically as

options.a: a labeling system for indifference curves.
options.b: a rule that makes every indifference curve linear.
options.c: a supply curve for consumption goods.
options.d: a replacement for the budget constraint.

questions.text: All bundles on the same indifference curve have

options.b: the same quantity of good 1.
options.c: the same utility level in a given utility representation.
options.d: the same marginal utilities for both goods.

questions.text: For u(x1,x2) = x1x2, an indifference curve at utility level k satisfies

options.c: x2 = kx1.

questions.text: On the nonnegative consumption set, v(x1,x2) = (x1x2)^2 represents the same preferences as u(x1,x2) = x1x2 because

options.b: squaring reverses the ranking of all bundles.
options.c: the two functions have identical marginal utility levels everywhere.
options.d: squaring is increasing for nonnegative utility values.

questions.text: Perfect-substitute preferences can be represented by

options.b: u(x1,x2) = x1/x2 necessarily.
options.c: u(x1,x2) = ax1 + bx2 with a,b > 0.
options.d: u(x1,x2) = v(x1) + x2 only if a = 0.

questions.text: For u(x1,x2) = ax1 + bx2, the slope of an indifference curve is

options.b: −b/a.
options.c: a + b.
options.d: −a/b.

questions.text: Perfect-complement preferences can be represented by

options.b: u(x1,x2) = ax1 + bx2.
options.c: u(x1,x2) = min(ax1,bx2) for positive a and b.

questions.text: In a perfect-complements utility function u = min(ax1,bx2), utility is limited by

options.a: the component available in the smaller effective proportion.
options.b: the sum of expenditures on both goods.
options.c: the larger of ax1 and bx2.
options.d: the good with the higher market price regardless of quantities.

questions.text: Quasilinear preferences can be represented by a utility function of the form

options.b: u(x1,x2) = min(x1,x2).
options.c: u(x1,x2) = x1x2 only.
options.d: u(x1,x2) = v(x1)x2 with no additive term.

questions.text: A characteristic feature of quasilinear indifference curves is that they are

options.b: parallel only when prices are equal.
options.c: L-shaped with a common kink.
options.d: vertical translations of one another.

questions.text: A Cobb-Douglas utility function has the form

options.b: u(x1,x2) = min(cx1,dx2).
options.c: u(x1,x2) = cx1 + dx2 only.

questions.text: Cobb-Douglas preferences are a standard example of

options.b: preferences with satiation at a finite point.
options.c: nontransitive preferences.
options.d: monotonic, convex, well-behaved preferences.

questions.text: Why can Cobb-Douglas exponents be normalized to sum to one without changing preferences?

options.a: The exponents are market prices and can be divided by income.
options.b: Any transformation, even a decreasing one, preserves preferences.
options.c: Only the sum of exponents affects the budget constraint.
options.d: A positive power transformation can rescale the exponents while preserving rankings.

questions.text: The marginal utility of good 1 is

options.a: the total derivative of income with respect to x1.
options.b: the partial derivative ∂u/∂x1, holding x2 fixed.
options.c: the slope of the budget line.
options.d: the ratio p1/p2.

questions.text: Marginal utility by itself has limited behavioral meaning because

options.a: its numerical magnitude changes under monotonic transformations of utility.
options.b: it is always zero at an optimum.
options.c: it depends only on prices, not preferences.
options.d: it cannot be computed from a differentiable utility function.

questions.text: For a differentiable utility function, the MRS of good 2 for good 1 is

options.b: p1 + p2 by definition.
options.c: MU1 + MU2.
options.d: −MU1/MU2.

questions.text: The MRS is invariant to a strictly increasing differentiable transformation of utility because

options.a: the MRS is defined without reference to preferences.
options.b: the common transformation factor cancels in the ratio of marginal utilities.
options.c: the transformation changes prices proportionally.
options.d: marginal utilities themselves are invariant.

questions.text: For Cobb-Douglas utility u = x1^c x2^d, the MRS is

options.d: −cd x1x2.

questions.text: In a linear estimated utility function for commuting characteristics, a coefficient can be interpreted as

options.a: the marginal utility weight placed on that characteristic.
options.b: the consumer’s total income.
options.c: the market price of that characteristic.
options.d: the probability of choosing public transport.

questions.text: In the commuting example U = −0.147TW − 0.0411TT − 2.24C, the negative coefficients on time and cost indicate that

options.a: commuters prefer longer trips and higher costs.
options.b: more walking time, travel time, or monetary cost lowers utility, other things equal.
options.c: utility is cardinally comparable across commuters.
options.d: time and cost are neutral characteristics.

questions.text: Ratios of coefficients in a linear utility model can be used to estimate

options.a: the number of consumers in the market.
options.b: the level of aggregate supply.
options.c: marginal rates of substitution between characteristics.
options.d: the slope of the consumer’s budget line only.

questions.text: Refer to the accompanying figure for u(x1,x2)=x1x2. Moving from the curve labeled k=1 to the curve labeled k=3 represents

options.a: a move to a lower utility level.
options.b: a move to a higher utility level and therefore to a more-preferred indifference curve.
options.c: a change in market prices rather than preferences.
options.d: no change in the preference ranking because all indifference curves have equal utility.

questions.text: If utility is multiplied by a positive constant, such as v = 5u, then

options.b: the represented preferences and the MRS are unchanged, although marginal utility numbers are multiplied by 5.
options.c: the represented preference ranking is reversed.
options.d: all indifference curves shift to different physical bundles.
